activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The ballot had been open in his browser for forty minutes, and Blake had read the candidate statements twice without anything resolving. His father wanted him to vote a straight ticket, the way the family always had, and had said so at dinner with the flat certainty of a man describing weather. His housemate from the group chat, Hamza, kept sending links that argued the opposite, each one more turgid than the last, dense with clauses that seemed designed to obscure rather than clarify. Between them sat Blake, eighteen years old, cursor hovering over a radio button, doing the thing he had waited his whole conscious life to do.

He had started the evening believing he knew his answer. Now he wasn't sure, and the uncertainty itself interested him, the way a hinge interests you once it squeaks. He opened a new tab, not to decide but to look sideways at the problem, and typed a question that had occurred to him in civics class: what happens in other countries if you don't vote?

The answer stopped him cold. Australia had used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who did not vote without a valid reason could be fined. He read it twice, then a third time, the way you reread a text from someone whose meaning you might have gotten wrong. Skipping a vote could cost money. Not metaphorically, not in the vague currency of civic guilt that teachers traded in, but actual dollars, an actual penalty. He tried to imagine his father's reaction if the state mailed him a fine for staying home. He tried to imagine his own.

He called Hamza, who picked up on the second ring with the wary tone of someone expecting another link.

"You know Australia fines people for not voting?" Blake said. "Since 1925. Federal elections. If you don't have a valid reason, you get fined."

There was a pause, the sound of a chair creaking, then Hamza's laugh, short and genuinely surprised. "Fined. Like a parking ticket."

"Like a parking ticket for apathy."

"That's either the best idea anyone's ever had or the worst one," Hamza said. "I can't tell which."

Neither could Blake, and that was the part he kept chewing on after they hung up. He sat with his hand on the mouse and let the two systems sit side by side in his mind. Here, voting was something you were invited to, wooed even, canvassed and advertised at and reminded about by celebrities. There, apparently, it was something owed, like taxes, like jury duty. His father treated voting as an inheritance, a thing handed down and not examined. Hamza treated it as a contest to be won. Neither of them seemed to treat it as a question.

I keep circling the same spot, Blake thought, and it was strange to notice himself noticing, like watching his own hands from a slight distance. The compulsory system assumed people would not show up unless made to. The voluntary system assumed the same thing, really, it just responded with persuasion instead of penalty. Both systems agreed on the problem. They disagreed about what a citizen was: someone who had to be convinced, or someone who owed. And underneath his frozen cursor, he realized, he had been waiting for someone to tell him which kind of citizen he was.

He thought about Ms. Swampy, his old neighbor, who had once watched him try to fix a rusted gate by painting over the corrosion. She had taken the wire brush from him without a word and started scraping. Some things you had to abrade before you could treat them; a coat of paint over rust only cauterized the surface, sealed the rot in place. His certainty about this ballot was rust. His father's certainty, Hamza's certainty, the whole noisy certainty of the internet, all of it paint over something no one wanted to scrape.

He closed the tab about Australia. Then he closed the tab with the turgid essays. He went back to the ballot and read the candidate statements one more time, slowly, and this time he let himself disagree with both his father and Hamza, out loud, in the empty room, just to hear what it sounded like. It sounded rough and unfinished, like a gate after scraping and before painting.

He didn't feel resolved. He felt like someone who had at least located the hinge.

He clicked the first radio button, then changed his mind, scrolled down, changed it back, and finally sat back with his hands off the keyboard entirely. His phone buzzed against the desk. Hamza: "so did you vote or are you waiting for them to invent the fine here first."

Blake laughed, put his fingers back on the keys, and typed, "still deciding. might be a while."

"You have until midnight."

"I know," Blake said, to the empty room, and clicked Submit.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
Kayla slid her registration card across the desk in Ms. Fischer's classroom before the bell, the laminate still stiff from the county office. "I need to leave during fourth period," she said. "The polls close at seven, but I work after school. This is my note."

Ms. Fischer turned the card over once, as if checking the back for something. "You realize you're the only senior who asked. Most of them aren't eighteen yet, and the ones who are mostly aren't bothering." She wrote the pass in green ink and handed it back. "Bring me the little sticker. I collect them."

Ronald leaned across the aisle as Kayla sat down. "You're actually going? For what? One vote out of a hundred thousand in this county. You could flip a coin a hundred thousand times and your coin wouldn't matter either." He had his boots up on the rung of his chair, the posture of someone who had thought about this enough to sharpen the argument and not enough to doubt it. He wanted her to stay, she had begun to realize, not because the argument was airtight but because Lauralie had already said she wasn't voting, and he didn't want to be the only one who had given up.

"It's not about being the deciding vote," Kayla said, and then stopped, because she wasn't sure what it was about, and she hated saying things she wasn't sure of.

Lauralie twisted around from the row in front. "It's about participating. Civic ritual. My mom says that." She made the word ritual sound like a disease.

What Kayla actually thought about was her grandfather, two summers ago, at the kitchen table with the fan clicking through its diurnal circuit of the room. She had said something careless, eighteen being basically still a kid, and he had set down his coffee. "They lowered the voting age to eighteen when I was in school," he said. "The people pushing for it had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Because eighteen-year-olds could be drafted for Vietnam. That's how we got the vote. Not by being wise. By being eligible to die." She had looked at his hands after that, the knuckles wide from forty years of work, and had not argued again.

The bell rang. Ms. Fischer was passing out the sample ballots she had requisitioned from the county office, a hundred of them in a cardboard box that still smelled of the print shop. "Mark them however you like," she said. "That's the point of a sample. Today we're going to argue the school board levy, and you're going to argue it as if your marks mattered, because next Tuesday they will."

They argued. Lauralie, who had started out shrugging, got caught somewhere in the middle of a point about the levy funding the metal detectors the school couldn't requisition on its own budget, and started talking faster, leaning forward, actually believing herself. Ronald argued the other side, taxes, his father's paycheck, and he was good at it, and Kayla watched him enjoy being good at it, and wondered whether he understood that this was the same thing as voting, just without the sticker.

When the clock moved toward fourth period, she stood, and Ronald said, quieter than before, "If it doesn't matter, why are you going?"

"That's the part I can't explain," Kayla said. "It matters that people fought to let me do it. It might matter more that I'm not sure it matters. Both of those can be true." She picked up her pass. "Somebody drafted at eighteen didn't get to be sure first."

The walk to the poll was eleven minutes in cold sun. Inside the fire station, a woman with a clipboard found her name, and another woman showed her to a machine that beeped when she touched the screen, a small obedient sound, and Kayla stood there a long moment with her finger hovering. Her grandfather had gotten the vote the way people get scars. She was getting it the way people get birthday presents. She could hold both of those without pretending they weighed the same, and she could still press the screen.

She wore the sticker back to Ms. Fischer's room before the final bell. Ronald was packing his bag, and he saw it and didn't say anything for a second.

"Next election I'll be nineteen," he finally said. "I'll still be in this town."

"Then you'll have no excuse," said Kayla, and pressed the sticker into the corner of his notebook, where it caught the light.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
Cohen had taken the job at the veterinary clinic because it paid eleven dollars an hour and because Mr. Buchanan, who owned the place, had told him during the interview that the work was mostly laundry. It was not mostly laundry. It was mopping kennels, holding dogs still for blood draws, and standing at the front desk while Mr. Buchanan dictated instructions Cohen was expected to remember without writing down.

On Thursday afternoons, a woman brought in her beagle for allergy shots, and while she waited she liked to quiz Cohen. She had seen him once with his biology textbook open on the counter and had appointed herself examiner. Today she leaned on the desk in her raincoat and asked what he was studying.

"DNA," Cohen said. "How it gets turned into protein."

"And you understand that?"

"I understand that I'm supposed to understand it by Tuesday."

She laughed and went back to her magazine, which was, in its way, the most honest thing anyone had said to him all week. The test was Tuesday. Finnegan had made a study group for Saturday and then discovered he had lacrosse, and Ludovic had offered to explain everything over the phone in eleven minutes, which Ludovic estimated was the time it would take, and which Cohen did not trust. He was alone with the textbook and the kennel noise.

The problem was not the words. He could recite the words. RNA polymerase, messenger RNA, transcription, translation. The problem was that the words sat in his head like a list of towns on a map he'd never driven. He wanted the shape of it, the reason.

In the back room, Mr. Buchanan was preparing a vaccine and narrating to no one in particular about a courier service he'd used in the city, how the original documents never left the archive, how copies went out. Cohen stood at the sink rinsing syringes and half listened. The clinic's own records lived in a locked cabinet in the office. The originals stayed there. When a specialist needed something, the office photocopied the page and sent that.

Cohen dried his hands slowly.

He thought about the cell keeping its DNA back, in the nucleus, in the archive, and sending out a copy. It would have been capricious of biology to do it the other way, shipping the original out into the cytoplasm where anything could happen to it. He pulled the textbook from his bag and set it on the steel counter beside the rabies pamphlets.

"RNA polymerase," he read, and then, testing it against the photocopy idea, said it aloud in his own words. The enzyme reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. The messenger carries the gene's instructions out. That was transcription. He said the word quietly, twice. Then translation, the copy being read at the ribosome, the protein being built. It was a working copy, not the archive itself.

Mr. Buchanan looked over. "You talking to yourself now?"

"Practicing for a test. Is it okay if I use the counter for ten minutes?"

"Long as the counter's clean."

Cohen spread his notes and made himself explain it, out loud, the way he'd explain it to someone who knew nothing. The consonance between the clinic's filing system and the cell's was so neat he distrusted it, an analogy being a kind of borrowed understanding, and he problematized it in the margin of his notebook, where the analogy fails, and found two places: the cell makes its copy with an enzyme, not a machine, and the copy is meant to be destroyed after use, which no archive would allow. He wrote those down too. The analogy carried him most of the way, and then it stopped carrying him, and past that point he had the textbook only.

A golden retriever named Tosca arrived at four for a torn nail, and Cohen held her while Mr. Buchanan trimmed and wrapped, and while he held her he kept whispering the sequence under his breath, polymerase, matching strand, messenger, out, translate, protein, until the woman in the raincoat's voice came from the waiting area.

"Is he still studying that DNA?"

"He is," Mr. Buchanan said.

"Ask him what a ribosome is, then."

"Ribosome," Cohen said, not looking up from Tosca's paw. "Where the message gets read and the protein gets built."

"See," the woman said to the room. "Tuesday's going to be fine."

Tosca licked his wrist. Mr. Buchanan taped the last of the wrap and said, "Kennel three needs new paper."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
story:
The argument started at 10:41 on a Tuesday night, when Philip posted the admission statistics for Ridgemont University into the group chat and typed, "so basically if you have the grades you're in." Alyssa was lying on her bed with her phone above her face, and she watched Alisha's reply arrive in three separate bubbles, the way she always typed when she was annoyed.

"that's not what it says." Then: "it says admitted students HAD the grades." Then: "that's different."

Alyssa sat up. She had been half watching a documentary about the sun, something about how its radiation could ionize the gases in the upper atmosphere and bend radio waves back toward earth, and the narrator's voice was still running in her head when she read the thread again. Philip was already going. "if every admitted student had a 3.8, then a 3.8 gets you admitted. that's just logic." Alisha answered with a single virulent "no it isn't," which in Alisha's vocabulary meant the conversation was about to become serious.

Alyssa typed slowly, then deleted it, then typed again. "ok but think about it with the sun." She paused, because it sounded strange even to her, and she could imagine Philip's face already. She sent it anyway. "for there to be direct sunlight, the sun has to be above the horizon, right." Philip sent back a shrugging emoji. She kept going. "but the sun being up doesn't mean you get direct sunlight. if you're standing behind a building, you're in shadow. the sun can be up and you still get nothing."

The typing indicator appeared and disappeared twice. Then Philip wrote, "cool story but we're talking about college." Alisha, though, sent a long message without her usual bubbles, all one piece: "wait. i think i see it. the sun being up is necessary. it has to hold or direct sunlight can't happen at all. but it's not sufficient. it can hold and you still don't get the thing, because something else can block it." Alyssa read it twice. That was exactly what she'd meant, said better than she'd said it, and she felt a small flush of vindication that she tried not to gloat over.

"so the grades are like the sun," she typed. "everybody admitted had them. they have to be there. but they don't guarantee anything. something else can cast a shadow. essays. luck. whatever." Philip went quiet for four minutes, long enough that Alyssa got up, found her brother's physics homework on the kitchen counter, and read a paragraph about a colloquialism, how people said the sun "rises" even though it was the earth turning, how convenient wrong language could be. When she came back Philip had written a paragraph.

"fine but then what's the point of working for grades at all. if they don't get you in, why am i doing two hours of calc a night." Alisha started to answer, something about how the alternative was worse, and Alyssa stopped her with a message she typed fast, before she could soften it. "because you can't even be in the running without them. they're the horizon. you're choosing to be someone the sun can reach." It was a weird sentence and she knew it, the kind of thing Mr. Byrne would circle in red if she put it in an essay, but Alisha sent back three exclamation points, which from Alisha was a standing ovation.

Philip didn't reply that night. The next morning in the hallway outside Mr. Byrne's room, he was waiting by the door with his phone out, and he held the screen toward her without saying hello. It was the university's admissions page, scrolled to a section titled "Holistic Review." "So I emailed them," he said. "Asked what a rejected applicant with a 4.0 looks like. Some admissions officer answered at like six in the morning." He scrolled to the reply, a paragraph of careful institutional language about how academic preparation was foundational but never the whole of a candidacy.

Alyssa read it twice. "She never actually says which part is the shadow," she said. "Essays, recommendations, they list everything, but they don't say what tips it." Philip pocketed the phone. "So we're back to not knowing." "We're back to knowing what we know," Alyssa said, and the bell rang, and they walked into the room still arguing about it.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Taylor arrived at the gym twenty minutes early, which she immediately regretted, because it gave her time to read her drill plan again and notice how bad it was. Eight lines of instructions for twelve eleven-year-olds, most of which began with the word "bend." Bend your wrists. Bend your knees. Bend your elbows, though not too much. She had written it like a manual for assembling a shelf, and the seventh-grade passing squad was not a shelf.

"You look dour," said Draven, dropping onto the bleachers beside her with a granola bar. "Like a Victorian portrait. Like someone canceled your birthday."

"My plan is wrong and I have eleven minutes."

"Wrong how?"

Taylor tapped the page. "Their passes die. Every drill I wrote fixes a body part instead of the pass." She said it and then heard it, the way you sometimes hear a sentence only after it leaves your mouth.

Over the summer, before anyone asked her to coach anything, Taylor had gone down a research rabbit hole that had metastasized from one article about free throws into a three a.m. spiral through motor learning studies, which Draven had later described as "the least fun anyone has ever had online." One finding had stuck: Gabriele Wulf's research found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, the target, rather than on their own body parts. Taylor had filed it away as trivia, the kind of thing that wins arguments at lunch and nowhere else.

"It's external focus," she said now, mostly to herself. "Wulf. Focus on where the ball goes, not on the wrist that throws it."

"So your whole plan is the wrong direction."

"My whole plan is a wrist museum."

Draven laughed so hard the granola bar was briefly at risk, and Taylor tore the page in half, which felt wonderful, and then wrote a new plan on the back of the halftime stats sheet, which felt less wonderful because it meant she had committed.

The kids came in at four, a herd of jerseys and untied shoes. Emmitt, who had agreed to help "for the entertainment value," set up three stations while Taylor gathered the players at half court. The shortest one, a girl with a mouthguard she did not need for basketball and wore anyway, looked up at Taylor with open, terrible trust.

"New plan," Taylor announced. "Nobody is going to mention wrists today. If anyone says wrist, they owe me a lap."

"What about elbows?" someone asked.

"Elbows, knees, shoulders, all banned. Today you only think about one thing: the ball hitting your teammate's hands."

"That's it?"

"That's it. Hit their hands. Nothing else exists."

The subtext of this, which Taylor understood and did not say, was that she was terrified. She had staked her one afternoon of authority on a study she'd read at three in the morning. If it failed, she would be the sixteen-year-old who told children to ignore their own bodies, and mouthguard girl would look at her with that same trust and be wrong to.

The first ten minutes were chaos regardless, because eleven-year-olds plus new instructions always equals chaos. One boy passed to where his teammate had been. Two girls got into a dispute about whether "hands" included "one hand." Emmitt refereed with the gravity of a UN delegate and the accuracy of a coin flip. Taylor kept her mouth shut about elbows, which was the hardest coaching she had ever done, because every mistake she saw came with a body part attached, begging to be named.

Then something shifted, and it was the mouthguard girl who did it. Standing at the third station, she stopped watching her own arms, stopped checking her feet, and just looked at her partner's hands, and the pass snapped out flat and clean, and her partner caught it without moving. The girl looked down at her hands as if they belonged to someone more talented.

"Did you see that?" she said.

"Again," said Taylor.

She did it again. Then again. By the end of the drill, four of the pairs were hitting hands so consistently that Emmitt had to keep backing up, complaining that he was becoming an encumbrance, an obstruction, a piece of furniture, and could someone acknowledge his sacrifice. Draven, keeping score from the bleachers, held up a sheet reading HITS: 38, WRISTS MENTIONED: 1, and under WRISTS MENTIONED someone had written "it was me, I'm sorry, I'm running my lap now."

The one lap-runner was the tallest boy, who had said "bend your wrist" to his partner in a moment of weakness, and who jogged the baseline with the dignity of a man serving an unjust sentence. When he came back, Taylor made him lead the next drill, calling targets aloud: "Hands, left. Hands, moving." He turned out to be the loudest and possibly best coach of the lot, once he was given something to say that wasn't anatomy.

At five thirty the parents started collecting players at the door like coats. Ms. He, who taught chemistry and had somehow ended up supervising the gym booking, came over with her clipboard and the expression of someone prepared to log a disaster. She watched mouthguard girl throw one last pass, flat and true, into her father's cupped hands as he walked in, entirely unaware he had become the final target of the day.

Ms. He looked at the torn plan on the floor, then at Taylor. "So what's the system?"

Taylor opened her mouth to explain, then found she didn't want to lecture anyone. She picked up the half page and held it out, crumpled, upside down, three a.m. ink and all.

"Hit the hands," she said. "Everything else is a lap."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
story:
The seminar room was spartan by decree of the budget office: one long table, chairs with cracked arms, a whiteboard that still held the ghost of last week's diagram. Mr. Dlamini had given them until four o'clock, ninety minutes, to prepare their cases for the exhibition debate on Saturday, and Isla had spent the first twenty of those minutes losing.

Marko had laid out his argument on the table like a hand of cards. "Every policy that reduces emissions is worth adopting at the national level. The carbon tax reduces emissions. Therefore the carbon tax is worth adopting at the national level." He said it evenly, without gloating, which somehow made it worse. Teresa, across the table, kept whispering that he was bluffing, that there had to be a hole somewhere, but Isla couldn't find it, and the clock above the door had already given up a third of its minutes.

She remembered, then, her mother's kitchen the summer before she left for college, the window open to the smell of cut grass, her mother saying that some fights you lose on purpose because winning them costs more than the fight is worth. Isla had been mesmerized by that at the time, by the idea of strategy shaped like surrender, and she had argued against it for an entire evening. She had wanted to be the kind of person who won fights outright. That seemed like a long time ago, from a chair in a room with a deadline.

"Run it again," she said to Marko. "Slowly. Every step."

"If all emissions-reducing policies are worth adopting nationally, and the tax reduces emissions, then the tax is worth adopting nationally." He tapped the whiteboard after each clause, as if the argument needed the percussion to hold together.

"If the premises are true, the conclusion follows," Isla said. "There's no hole in the shape of it." She felt the truth of this like a stone in her shoe. She had been trained to hunt for fallacies, for leaps, and here was a chain with no missing links.

"So you concede," Marko said.

"No." She stood, because sitting she could only think in his rhythm. "Valid isn't the same as sound. A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true. Yours is valid. It isn't sound."

Mr. Dlamini, who had been leaning by the door in his rain jacket, said nothing, but he uncrossed his arms, which from him was applause.

"Which premise is false," Teresa said, not quite a question, already flipping her notes.

"Every emissions-reducing policy is worth adopting at the national level. That's just not true." Isla wrote it on the board and underlined it twice, hard enough that the marker squealed. "Some policies that reduce emissions are worth adopting locally, or regionally, and would fail at the national level. Some of them cost more elsewhere than they save. He's dressed an ordinary claim up as a universal one, and the artifice only shows at that one premise, so that's where you hit it." She turned to Marko. "I don't have to break your argument. I only have to break one brick."

Marko looked at the board for a long moment. "Twenty minutes to rebuild," he said, and began erasing his own case from his notes, which was, Isla thought, the most generous thing an opponent had ever done for her.

They rebuilt it together, which the exhibition rules did not forbid and Mr. Dlamini did not discourage. Marko narrowed his first premise until it was too modest to attack and too weak to do much, and Teresa drafted questions that would force him to defend the weaker version in public. At four o'clock exactly, Mr. Dlamini collected their cases, read both sides in silence, and told them it was the best work any of them had done all term. Walking out into the corridor, Isla was still riding it, the clarity, the feeling of having found the one loose thread in a whole woven thing.

That night, at her laptop, she opened her own case to polish it, and read the first premise the way she had read Marko's: slowly, every step. Voters reward parties that lower household costs. Lowering household costs requires the carbon tax. Therefore voters will reward the party that passes the carbon tax. Valid, she saw at once, valid as a straight edge. And then she sat very still, because the second premise was one she had never checked, only believed, the way Marko had believed his universal, and Saturday was three days away, and her whole case stood on it.

She picked up her phone. "Marko," she said. "Do you still have the household cost data?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The smell of her grandmother's cardamom tea drifted into the den, where Hannah's grandfather had arranged the chairs in a semicircle around the television like a small stadium of their own. It was the conference championship, and everyone had come: her parents, her aunt and uncle, Greyson from down the street, Umar with the buffalo dip he'd made from his mother's recipe, and the smallest cousin, Nadia, who was seven and had staked out the best spot on the carpet.

Hannah had promised herself she would figure out why she was here. She didn't love football the way Greyson did, didn't understand the coverage schemes Umar and her uncle argued about at every commercial break. But she wanted to belong to this room, to the noise it made, and that want had felt flimsy all week, the kind of thing that dissolved when anyone asked her a direct question about the game.

"Watch this," Greyson said, leaning toward her during a lull in the third quarter. "Fourth and one. They'll go for it."

On the screen, the yellow stripe stretched across the field, marking the distance to a first down. Nadia sat up suddenly, pointing at it with a chip in her hand. "Why do they paint the line only sometimes? It moves. Who paints it so fast?"

Hannah opened her mouth to say nobody knew, and then closed it, because the question snagged on something. The line moved between plays. It appeared and vanished. Grass did not do that. Painters did not do that, not in thirty seconds, not in a stadium of cameras watching. "It's not paint," she said slowly, testing it. "I don't think it's on the field at all."

"It's painted," Nadia insisted, and turned to Greyson for backup.

Greyson frowned at the screen, then at the players, whose cleats crossed the yellow stripe without disturbing it. Umar paused mid-argument with the uncle. Hannah pulled out her phone, half hoping to be wrong, because being wrong in front of Nadia felt like a small betrayal of a seven-year-old's whole worldview. She typed the question and read, and read again, and started to laugh quietly into her sleeve.

"It's drawn by a computer," she said. "The yellow line isn't really there. It was first shown on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision." She said it twice, softer the second time, for Nadia, who was frowning at the screen as though it had lied to her personally.

Nadia absorbed this with visible suspicion. "So the players can't see it?"

"Only we can see it," Hannah said. "The people in the stadium don't get the line. We know something they don't, sitting right here with the dip."

Nadia considered this for a long moment, then scooted backward until she was leaning against Hannah's chair, which she had never done before. Hannah's grandmother came through with the tea, and Ms. Siddiqui from next door, who had heard the cheering through the shared wall and brought a plate of baklava, munificent as always, refusing all thanks. She settled into the last chair and asked Nadia what she was studying so hard.

"The yellow line," Nadia said. "It's a lie that helps."

Everyone laughed, but Hannah kept turning the phrase over. A lie that helps. She thought about how the whole afternoon ran on things like that: her uncle narrating certainty he didn't have, Greyson's confident predictions that came true maybe half the time, the replay angles that turned a dropped pass into a heroic attempt. Her father, who knew she hadn't wanted to come today, had said nothing about it all afternoon, only kept refilling her glass, an offer of peace he hadn't put into words.

"It problematizes the whole broadcast, doesn't it," Umar said, gesturing at the screen with a celery stick. "If they can draw a line that isn't there, what else are we accepting on faith?"

"The line's real," Greyson said. "It's just not painted. There's a difference."

"Is there?" Umar said, and Hannah let them have it, because she was less interested in winning the point than in holding both of them at once. The line was a fiction, and it told the truth: the distance was real, the measurement was real, and what the computer drew was honest in a way that confused her pleasantly. She thought of her own presence in the room the same way. She didn't love football; she loved this. Both things were true and neither one canceled the other, and she decided she could stop needing a cleaner reason.

In the fourth quarter the home team drove down the field, and the yellow line crept closer to the end zone, and Nadia tracked it like a hawk, announcing each time the invisible painters had done their work. When the receiver stretched across the goal line with the ball, the room detonated, and Ms. Siddiqui's baklava nearly went airborne, and Nadia leapt up and shouted, "THAT one was real!" Hannah picked her up before she could knock over the dip, and Nadia, arms around her neck, whispered, "Sit by me next game?"

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Tristan had both articles open on the library computer, side by side, and both were telling him the truth. The first, by a sociologist, argued that school start times had no measurable effect on adolescent grades. The second, by a team of education researchers, claimed the opposite. He checked the dates, the journals, the sample sizes; he looked for some flaw that would let him dismiss one of them. Neither crumbled. He was supposed to have a critical review finished by the end of the period, comparing the two, and so far he had produced one sentence, which he deleted.

"You look like you're trying to extrude a whole essay through your eyeballs," Shannon said, sliding into the chair beside him with a carton of chocolate milk. She leaned over and scanned his screen. "Still the start times thing?"

"They contradict each other. Completely. And they both look competent." He pulled up the first article again, its tables dense with numbers he only half understood. "Ms. Krause said a critical review means taking a position, not just summarizing both sides. But how am I supposed to take a position when the evidence points two ways?"

Shannon slurped her milk with terrible deliberation. "Maybe that's the position. That it's unresolved."

"That's relativism," Tristan said. "That's the thing she said not to do. Just shrugging and saying everyone's right."

The clock above the returns desk showed twenty minutes left in the period. Down the hall he could hear Ms. Krause's class shuffling papers, and he knew she'd be at the library doors at the bell, collecting drafts from the students who'd chosen to work there. He typed "school start times adolescent grades" into the database search and then, on a hunch he couldn't fully justify, added the word "pooled."

The result that came up was titled like a question being settled. A meta-analysis, the abstract began, of forty-one studies. He read the line twice. The word was familiar from somewhere, maybe a footnote he'd skipped, but the sentence that followed laid it out plainly: a meta-analysis combined the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could. He sat back. It was like zooming out on a map until both towns he'd been comparing turned out to be in the same country.

"It's a meta-analysis," he said.

"It's a what?"

"A study of studies. It takes all the single ones, the ones arguing with each other, and pools them. Any one article can be off, small sample, weird luck. But if you put them together, the overall effect gets estimated more precisely than any single study can manage." He was talking fast now, half to Shannon, half to the machine. "Both my articles were single studies. No wonder they disagreed. They were each too small to see the whole shape."

Shannon tilted the carton and got only air. "So which one does the pooled one agree with?"

He found the results section and ran his finger down the screen. A small positive effect on grades. Small, but there, once everything was combined. The education researchers had the direction right; the sociologist's null finding was what a single study could easily show even when a real effect existed, a fragment of the picture mistaken for the whole. But the effect was modest, the paper was careful to say, smaller than the second article's confident tone had implied. So neither article was simply wrong, and neither was simply right, and the honest position was somewhere layered: the question was mostly settled by pooling, the size of the answer was still being argued.

He started writing, and the paragraphs came out faster than they had all week, though the friable parts, the claims he'd built on the sociologist alone, kept crumbling as he typed over them. Marika appeared at the end of the table, dropping her bag. "Krause is at the door," she said. "Three minutes."

He wrote the final sentence, that his position rested on the pooled estimate but that he trusted the precision only so far, and that what stayed uncertain was whether the modest effect mattered to any particular school. It felt strange to end on an admission rather than a verdict, like leaving a door open on purpose. He hit print and stood while the machine groaned somewhere behind the front desk.

Shannon walked with him toward the doors, where Ms. Krause was already holding out her hand for the stack of drafts. "You realize," Shannon said, "you spent forty minutes stuck and seven minutes writing."

"It wasn't seven," Tristan said, and handed his pages over, still warm.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
story:
The city archive closed at five, which gave Landon exactly three hours to figure out which of his two historians was lying to him, or whether neither was, which felt worse. He spread the photocopies across a table under a humming fluorescent light: an excerpt from Professor Harcourt, who called the McCarthy era a travesty built on paranoia and ruined lives, and an excerpt from Dr. Kellerman, who argued that American fears of Soviet espionage had been substantially justified. His essay was due at eight the next morning. Mr. Ahmadi had assigned it as an exercise in judgment, not summary. "Anyone can report what historians say," he had told the class. "I want to know what you say, once you've checked them against the evidence."

Brock slid into the chair across from him and dropped a granola bar on the table like an offering. "I came to watch you lose," he said. "You've been glaring at those pages like they insulted your mother."

"They insulted each other. Harcourt says the spy scare was mass hysteria. Kellerman says Harcourt is naive." Landon tapped the pages. "One of them has to be wrong about the facts, but they're both, like, decorated professors. How am I supposed to referee two professors by tomorrow?"

Sophia arrived with a cardboard box she'd requested from the front desk and set it down with the reverence of someone carrying a sleeping infant. "Mr. Ahmadi pulled these for us," she said. "He says if we finish before five, he'll show us the basement where they keep the fire insurance maps from 1898, which I personally care about more than the Cold War, no offense to the dead Russians." Her actual project was on the archive's founding donors, and she had her own deadline, a presentation at Monday's history club that she kept mentioning so nobody would forget it.

"Offense taken on behalf of the dead Russians," Landon said, and lifted the box lid. Inside were folders of declassified documents, and near the top, a pamphlet with a cover that read, in bureaucratic gray, Venona Decrypts, Released 1995. He read the first page and felt something in his chest palpitate, which he chose to interpret as scholarly excitement rather than the granola bar Brock had made him share earlier. The pamphlet described decrypted Soviet intelligence messages, and the release date meant something he turned over slowly, the way you test a loose tooth.

"Wait," he said. "Harcourt's book. What year was it published?"

Sophia flipped to his bibliography page. "Nineteen eighty-seven," she said, then looked up. "Oh. Oh, that's interesting."

"That's interesting is right." Landon pulled Harcourt's excerpt back in front of him. Harcourt had written, confidently, that no direct evidence of extensive Soviet spy networks in America had ever surfaced, that the accusations rested on suspicion and forgery. He had written it in 1987. The Venona decrypts had been released by the US government in 1995, eight years later, and they confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States. Harcourt couldn't have seen them. He wasn't lying. He was just writing from before the ground moved.

"So Kellerman wins?" Brock leaned back, chair creaking. "Case closed, essay done in one paragraph, let's go get food."

But Landon was already shaking his head, because Kellerman's excerpt had its own problem. Kellerman leaned on the decrypts like a man leaning on a fence that might not hold him, stretching them to defend accusations that, even in the pamphlet's careful language, had targeted people who were never spies at all. "Kellerman treats the confirmation as if it retroactively justifies everything anyone ever alleged," Landon said. "That's specious. The networks were real, sure, but half the people McCarthy named weren't in them. Both things can be true."

"Both things can be true," Sophia repeated, writing it down. "That's going in my presentation. About the donors, obviously, but still."

"You cannot steal my conclusion for your donor presentation, Sophia." But he said it without heat, because his pen was already moving across the essay's opening paragraph, the one he'd rewritten four times at home and now saw clearly for the first time. Harcourt was honest but underinformed; Kellerman was informed but overreaching; the evidence itself, the decrypts, confirmed the networks without confirming every accusation. What stayed uncertain was the space in between, the question of how a country tells real danger from invented danger when both are in the room, and Landon wrote a full paragraph admitting he didn't know, and marked it with a star so he wouldn't quietly delete it later out of cowardice.

At four forty, Mr. Ahmadi appeared at their table with a ring of keys and an expression of rehearsed boredom that fooled nobody. "You have eleven minutes," he said. "The fire insurance maps await." He glanced at Landon's marked-up pages, the two excerpts, the pamphlet lying open between them like a verdict that refused to be simple, and one eyebrow moved a fraction of a millimeter, which from Mr. Ahmadi was applause. "You found Venona on your own, then."

"He found it, I stole his conclusion, and Brock provided snacks," Sophia said, closing her donor folder with dignity.

Brock held up the empty granola wrapper as evidence. The fluorescent light buzzed. Somewhere below them, Mr. Ahmadi's keys were already turning in the door to the basement.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: In the far North Atlantic, the water cools and becomes dense enough to sink, then flows south deep underwater as part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
story:
The quarry had filled with spring rain years before Hailey was born, and the town had never decided whether it was a hazard or a swimming hole, so it remained both. She sat on the flat slab at the south edge with a laminated ocean current map spread across her knees, its red and blue arrows looping like something spilled. Tomorrow at eight she would stand in the museum's auditorium and explain, in under ten minutes, how a current off the coast of Florida keeps Britain from having winters like Newfoundland's. She had exactly one night to understand it.

"You brought homework to a quarry," Cara said, wringing out her hair. She and Coen had been in the water twice already. Below the surface the quarry was unnaturally cold, the kind of cold that grabbed at the ankles, and the cliffs around it gave everything a lugubrious green light, as if the whole place were remembering a funeral.

"I brought the Gulf Stream," Hailey said. "Look. Warm water rides north along the eastern seaboard, then bends east toward Europe. Same latitude, completely different climate. Palm trees in Ireland." She traced the red ribbon with her finger and stopped where it ended, in the far North Atlantic, where the red simply quit. That was the part she couldn't explain. Where did all that warm water go? Her notes had a phrase in them, copied from a museum placard, and every time she read it the words slid apart on her.

Coen dropped his towel beside her and leaned over the map, dripping. "What's that snake one called? Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation." He read it off the legend like a dare, then looked up. "That's a real thing? It sounds like something you'd ascribe to a wizard."

"It's real. I just don't know what it does." She said this flatly, but the flatness was work. She had been at the science museum on Tuesday, alone, watching the big projection of the North Atlantic. In the animation the red current had reached the far northeast, turned blue, and then, instead of stopping, it had dived. It had gone straight down and turned south again, deep underwater, a ribbon flowing home in the dark. She'd stood there through two full loops of the animation, and she'd walked out without writing down why. Free admission on Tuesdays, Coen called it, was arbitrage; she never paid for what she could learn standing still. But this time she'd gambled and lost, and tomorrow was the deadline.

Cara had gone quiet in a way Hailey registered only later. She was sitting on the rock wall now, fully dressed again, her wet suit folded under her, watching the water rather than the map. "Are you going in again?" Coen asked her, and Cara said, "Not tonight," and turned the question around, asked Hailey how long the presentation was, whether the whole class would be there, whether the judges were the same ones from last year. The questions came a little too fast, and Hailey answered them while looking at the map, where the red current ended in that blank northern water, and something began to assemble itself.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Watch. The water goes north, warm, red, all that heat handed off to the winds that hit Europe. Then it gets up there and it cools." She put her finger on the northeast corner of the map. "And cold water is heavier. It becomes dense enough to sink. It goes down, and it flows south again, deep underwater, back the whole way it came. That's the circulation. That's the overturning. It doesn't end, it just goes dark." She looked up. "That's why the animation turned blue and dove. It wasn't broken."

"That's it?" Coen said. "You've been agonizing since Tuesday over that?"

"There's a difference between knowing what happens and knowing why I believe it," Hailey said, and then, because that sounded like a poster, she started folding the map. She still wasn't sure about the parts her notes glossed over, the parts where the museum placard had implied more than it said, and she was honest enough to plan on saying so tomorrow: here is what the map shows, here is what I can defend, here is what I can't. She believed the sinking water; she could not yet say she understood it.

Cara stood, hugging her folded suit. "You should know something before tomorrow," she said. "I submitted too." The museum had allowed two entries per school, but the auditorium held one presenter, and the selection email had gone out that afternoon while Hailey was printing her map. Cara's phone was in her hand, screen dark, and she didn't turn it over. Coen whistled low at the water. "So who got it?" he said, but he was looking at Hailey when he asked, and nobody answered, and the quarry held its cold and its light and said nothing either.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The booking confirmation sat on Audrey's phone like a dare: test in six weeks, first lesson this morning, nine o'clock, in the driveway of the house on Fenwick Road. She had chosen the automatic option when she filled in the form, partly because the slider on the website made it look like the sensible choice, partly because her mother had said, twice, that learning in a manual was a rite of passage nobody needed anymore. The school's car would arrive glossy and dual-controlled, and for six weeks Audrey would not have to think about a clutch.

At five to nine she was standing on the driveway in her jacket, and the instructor's car pulled in behind her mother's aging Astra, which was, her mother liked to remind her, a manual, and the only car the family owned. The instructor introduced herself as Ms. Katz, checked Audrey's provisional licence with the thoroughness of a customs officer, and asked her to name the controls. Audrey managed most of them. The pedals in an automatic were fewer, which felt like being handed a shorter exam.

"Right," Ms. Katz said. "Handbrake off, foot on the brake, into drive, and we'll just roll to the end of the road."

Rolling turned out to be a generous word for it. The car crept, lurched, stopped, crept again, while Audrey tried to verbalize what her feet were doing, because Ms. Katz insisted she narrate. "Braking. Still braking. Now the accelerator, gently." The gentle part took three attempts. By the end of the hour she had driven around the block twice, mounted a kerb once, and learned that indicators cancel themselves, which struck her as the car showing off.

Back in the driveway, engine ticking as it cooled, Kaiya cycled past and stopped at the gate, one foot on the tarmac. "Automatic, yeah?" Kaiya said, nodding at the school car. "Smart. Frank's doing manual and he says the clutch is going to end him."

"Six weeks to my test," Audrey said. "That's the smart part."

"Six weeks," Kaiya repeated, as though tasting it. "Frank says if you pass in an automatic you can only drive automatics. Like, ever. Is that true?"

Ms. Katz was writing something on a clipboard and did not look up, but she said, without ceremony, "Pass in an automatic, you're licensed for automatics only. You'd have to take another test to drive a manual."

Audrey looked down the driveway at the Astra, its gears, its three pedals, the only car she would actually be allowed to drive past her test date if she did this the easy way. Six weeks. The next available manual lesson with the school, she would later learn, was eleven days out, because everyone else's mother had apparently not had the same thought about rites of passage.

From the kitchen window, Ms. Katz watched the two girls by the gate while she filled in the progress sheet. The pupil had decent observation, poor throttle control, and a habit of apologising to the car, which Ms. Katz had seen before and considered a better sign than swearing. She could see the girl doing arithmetic on her fingers, practically: the test date, the family car, the second test she would have to sit if she took the smooth road now. Pupils always thought the choice was about gears. It was never about gears. It was about whether six weeks of one kind of difficulty was worth avoiding an interminable second round of forms and waiting lists and reversing around corners in a car that fought back.

Ms. Katz had been teaching for nineteen years, and she had developed a private jurisprudence on the subject: never advise, only inform, because advice given in a driveway was advice resented at a roundabout. She capped her pen and went out to move the car.

Audrey was still at the gate, and Kaiya had gone, and her mother had come out with a mug of tea and was looking at the Astra with the fondness people reserve for things that are about to become someone else's problem.

"Could I learn in yours?" Audrey said. "The Astra. On the driveway, before the lessons switch over."

Her mother sipped her tea. "The clutch is heavy."

"I know it's heavy. Everyone keeps telling me it's heavy."

"It stalled on me in 2014 at a junction and a man got out of his van to help."

"Did it help?"

"It made it worse," her mother admitted, and there was a silence in which the two of them looked at the car, and the car sat there being old and manual and the only option, and Audrey thought about Frank's doomed clutch and Kaiya's question and the slider on the website, and did not yet know whether she had chosen wrong or only chosen early. Ms. Katz's car started behind them with a polite cough.

"Lesson same time Thursday," Ms. Katz said through the window. "Automatic. Unless you ring the office."

Audrey held her mother's car keys up, and the morning light caught them. "Show me the biting point," she said.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: A 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters.
story:
Coralie had the ocean current map pinned to the wall of the science room before first period, tracing the red ribbon of the Gulf Stream with her finger as it swung away from Florida and aimed itself at Europe like an arrow. Her report was due Thursday. She had written four pages arguing that warm water carried north across the Atlantic was the reason London winters were milder than Halifax's, even though both cities sat at nearly the same latitude. She was proud of those four pages. She had drawn her own map, copied the currents in colored pencil, and practiced saying "thermohaline circulation" without stumbling.

Emrik came in with his laptop under his arm and sat two desks away, which was how he sat, close enough to talk, far enough to pretend he wasn't. He opened the laptop and started typing without looking at her wall.

"You should check something," he said after a while. He turned the screen toward her. She read the first lines of an abstract, a 2002 study led by a man named Richard Seager, and then she stopped reading, because the first lines were enough. The study argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters. She read the sentence twice. Then she read it a third time, slowly, as if the words might rearrange themselves.

"That can't be right," she said. "Every textbook says the Gulf Stream."

"Read the rest."

"I have practice," she said, but she didn't move.

Ms. De Vries came in at the bell and asked who was ready for Thursday. Coralie raised her hand, and her hand felt like it belonged to someone more certain than she was. Ms. De Vries nodded and moved on to Hugh, who was doing his report on tides and had built a model out of a cake pan and a hair dryer. Coralie spent the class taking notes on tides she already understood, and the Seager sentence sat in her head the way a stone sits in a shoe. Not painful, exactly. Just impossible to ignore.

After school she found Emrik in the library and made him pull the study up again. They read it together at a carrel near the window, passing the laptop back and forth. Hugh found them there, looked over Coralie's shoulder, and said, "So the Gulf Stream's a myth?"

"No," Coralie said. "That's not what it says." She pointed at the sentence. "It says more than. Not only. There's a difference."

Hugh shrugged and went to find a book about undertow. Emrik watched her read. "You going to change your report?"

"Ms. De Vries said a report has to take a position," she said. She sounded more confident than she felt, and she disliked the sound of her own voice for it.

That night she laid the colored pencil map on her bedroom floor and looked at it. Four pages. She could submit it Thursday, get the grade, and be done. Her father came by the door and asked how the report was going, and she said fine, and he went to bed with the stoicism of a man who had learned not to ask twice. She stayed on the floor. The map hadn't changed. The red ribbon still crossed the Atlantic. The problem was that the map showed one true thing, and the study showed another true thing, and she had built four pages on the idea that only one truth could fit on a page.

She started a fifth page at eleven. She wrote that the Gulf Stream carried heat north, and that this was real, and drawn on every map she'd found. Then she wrote the Seager sentence in her own words: that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters. She sat with both claims in front of her and did not try to force them into one. She wrote that the question was which mattered more, and that she wasn't sure the question had a clean answer, and that a clean answer might not be the same as a true one.

Thursday came. Ms. De Vries called her name, and Coralie walked to the front carrying the colored pencil map and the fifth page, which was now the last page. She talked about latitude and London and Halifax. She traced the red ribbon with the same finger as before. Then she said, "But a 2002 study by Richard Seager says winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters. So my first four pages are half the story." She looked at Emrik, who was sitting two desks away, and he gave her the smallest nod. Ms. De Vries wrote something on her clipboard.

"You're sanguine about losing half your argument," Ms. De Vries said.

"I'm honest about it," Coralie said. "The Gulf Stream warms Europe. It also doesn't explain most of it. Both of those are in the evidence, and I don't think I get to pick the one I like." She folded the map along its crease and set it on the desk. "The line that delimits the two claims is somewhere, and I can't say exactly where. But it's not where my textbook drew it."

Ms. De Vries asked the class if anyone had a question. Hugh raised his hand and asked whether the cake pan and hair dryer counted as a model or a toy.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
The cafe on Delmore Street had one long table by the window, and Daniel spread his articles across it before his latte had even cooled: two photocopies, one flagged with green sticky notes, one with pink. Across the top of his notebook he had written, in the optimistic script of a person who had not yet started, "Critical Review: Article A vs. Article B." Below that, nothing.

Thalia dropped her bag on the chair opposite him and peered at the pages upside down. "You're still on that? Ma assigned it two weeks ago."

"I've been reading," Daniel said. "I just haven't been writing."

"That's a distinction without a difference." She unwrapped a muffin and, because she was Thalia, pulled the pink-flagged article toward herself anyway. "What's this one?"

"A review of the MMR controversy. Epidemiological. They pooled a bunch of large studies, hundreds of thousands of kids, and found no association between the vaccine and autism." He tapped the green one. "This is a history-of-science piece about the original paper, the one that started everything."

"Started what?"

"The claim. The Lancet, 1998. Wakefield. That's the part I keep circling." He turned to a page he had underlined twice, which he almost never did. "The whole thing was based on twelve children."

Thalia stopped chewing. "Twelve."

"Twelve children." He said it slowly because he was still absorbing the arithmetic himself. "And this other article, the epidemiology one, is working from sample sizes in the hundreds of thousands. So the comparison isn't just two answers to the same question. It's two entirely different ideas of what counts as evidence." He pulled the notebook toward him and wrote, finally: "What makes a study believable: its size, or its novelty?"

"Neither," said Mataya, arriving with an iced coffee and no greeting, which was Mataya's way. She sat down at the end of the table and put her feet on the rung of Daniel's chair. "Credibility is about method."

"Then why did anyone believe the small one for a decade?"

"Because people interpolate," Mataya said. "They take twelve kids and imagine a pattern that stretches across every kid they know. That's not evidence, that's arithmetic done by fear." She stole a corner of Thalia's muffin. "Write that down, it's better than your sentence."

Daniel did not write it down. Instead he sat back and looked at the window, at the bus shelter across the street, and remembered being nine, in his pediatrician's waiting room, while his mother argued with the receptionist. He could still see the woman's laminated schedule of shots on the counter, and his mother's finger tapping a line she did not want signed. There had been a magazine on the chair beside him with a cover about the vaccine debate, and he had read the word "controversy" and understood, at nine, that this was a thing adults were afraid of on his behalf. He had gotten the shot anyway. He remembered the sting and his mother's face afterward, relieved and stubborn at once, as if she had granted the needle some grudging clemency.

"Where did you go?" Thalia asked.

"Nowhere. My mom almost didn't vaccinate me." He picked up his pen. "That's actually the problem with my draft. Or my non-draft. I keep wanting to write the review like a verdict. Like the point is to convict the twelve-child paper and acquit the big one."

"Isn't it?" Mataya said.

"Not exactly. The history article says something weirder. It says the small study mattered because of how it was handled afterward, the press, the retractions, all of it. The big numbers only got assembled because the small claim existed. So which article do I trust more? The one with better evidence, or the one that explains why the worse evidence won attention?" He wrote a second line under the first: "The review has to hold both."

Mr. Ma came in at four, as he did most afternoons, ordered his flat white, and noticed Daniel's fortress of paper on the way to the counter. He raised his eyebrows at it.

"Progress?" he asked.

"Two paragraphs," Daniel said, which was true as of ten minutes ago.

"Effusive, I hope."

"Restrained, actually."

"Even better." Mr. Ma collected his cup and left without further comment, which Daniel appreciated, because the worst possible thing at this stage would have been advice.

He wrote until six. The review took shape around a hinge he had not expected: a paragraph on the twelve children, stated plainly, followed by a paragraph on the studies with samples in the hundreds of thousands, and then the admission that he could not fully reconcile them, that the second article's rigor was a response to the first article's flaw, and that this made them not opposites but a sequence. Thalia read it over his shoulder and said it sounded like a person thinking, which he decided was a compliment. Mataya said the last sentence was doing too much work, and he cut it. At half past six he emailed the file to himself, packed up the flags and the photocopies, and left the table cleaner than he had found it.

Outside, at the bus shelter, a woman was telling a younger man, in the patient over-articulate voice of someone delivering wisdom, that he should look into the vaccine studies himself before trusting doctors, because the original research had raised real questions. Daniel stood beside them holding his folder of two articles, one of which had taken that research apart, and the woman turned to him, gesturing at the toddler sleeping in her stroller, and asked, "You're a student, right? Would you give it to your own kid?"

He looked at her, then at his folder, and said, "Which study are you asking about?"

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership, and the number of station owners then fell sharply even as the number of stations grew.
story:
The radio in Audrey's mother's car had two presets, one for their town and one for her aunt's city four hours north, and last summer Audrey had noticed that the same morning show came out of both. Same host, same jokes, same phone-number song. She had asked her mother why, and her mother said maybe they syndicated it, and Audrey had let it go. Now Ms. Paquette had put a radio ownership chart on the projector in media studies, and Audrey was copying it into her notebook without understanding it.

"Pick a medium," Ms. Paquette said. "Any medium. Find out who owns it, then find out who owns them. That's your project. Presentations start Thursday."

Desiree leaned across the aisle. "I'm doing TikTok, obviously."

"I'll do magazines," Coraline said. "The florid ones at the checkout, the ones about royal babies. Someone prints those. Someone decides there should be forty of them."

Audrey looked at the chart again. It listed radio stations on one axis and station owners on another, two lines moving in different directions, and something about the shape of it bothered her in a way she could not yet name. She raised her hand. "Can I do radio?"

"You can do radio," Ms. Paquette said, and moved on to a boy arguing that podcasts counted as a medium.

After school, Audrey sat in the public library with three browser tabs open and her notebook flat beside the keyboard. She found the phrase first, on a page about regulation: the Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. She wrote it down. Then she found the numbers, and they were strange enough that she checked them twice. Before the act, a company could own only so many stations across the whole country. After the act, there was no cap at all. And then the number of owners fell, sharply, while the number of stations kept growing. More stations, fewer people deciding.

She remembered the car, the same host in two cities, and felt the two things click together, though not into anything tidy. She texted her mother: why do your two presets have the same show. Her mother replied with a shrugging emoji and then, in a second message, I never thought about it, they're just the stations.

At lunch the next day she spread her notebook between Desiree's tray and Coraline's.

"So there's no limit anymore," Audrey said. "On how many radio stations one company can own in the country. Since the act. And then more stations existed but fewer companies owned them."

"Which means what, exactly?" Desiree asked.

"Maybe nothing. Maybe it means my aunt and my mom hear the same show because someone bought the same station in both places. Or maybe the show was syndicated anyway, like TV reruns, and the ownership thing is separate. I keep trying to transmute the numbers into an answer and they won't go."

Coraline tapped the notebook. "But somebody picked those numbers to be legal. Somebody lobbied for that."

"That part I believe," Audrey said. "What I can't prove is that it changed what gets said on the air. I only know it changed who's able to say it."

Desiree frowned at her sandwich. "You're going to stand up Thursday and tell the class you don't know?"

"I'm going to tell them what the lines on the chart are, and then tell them the part I'm not sure about. That's different."

The night before her presentation, Audrey made two lists on index cards. One said what she knew: the cap eliminated by the act, owners falling, stations growing, the same host on two dials four hours apart. The other said what she didn't: whether the sameness came from ownership or from cheaper programming, whether fewer owners meant fewer viewpoints or only fewer paychecks. She stared at the second card for a long time, because it felt like a weakness, and then decided it was more like the opposite, a door she hadn't walked through yet and was admitting existed.

On Thursday she stood at the front with the chart projected behind her, the two lines going their separate ways, and told the class the plain facts. Then she said, "The same morning show plays in my town and in my aunt's city, and I used to think that was just how radio worked. Now I think somebody made it that way, and I can name the year the rules changed, but I can't tell you what would have played otherwise. Nobody kept a tape of the show that didn't happen."

A boy in the back raised his hand. "So is the news on those stations slanted, or not?"

"I'd want to know who owns the station before I answer," Audrey said, "and then I'd still want to check it against a station someone else owns. My whole position is that it's two checks, not one."

Ms. Paquette wrote something on her clipboard. Audrey sat down. Coraline passed her a folded note, and Audrey opened it under her desk: "You used more 'I don't knows' than anyone. It sounded like the strongest one up there." Audrey folded it back along its crease and put it in her pocket, and when the bell rang she was still holding her index cards, the second one face up on the desk.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
The application took eleven minutes at the customer service desk, most of it spent waiting for the printer. Nevaeh had written her availability in careful print, every Sunday, every evening after four, and when the manager, Mr. Tan, read it over, he said, "You'll be stocking and bagging. It starts at seven twenty-five." She signed the line he pointed to without doing any math.

Laeticia had a job too, at a supermarket one town over, except her town sat just across the state line. They had applied the same week in September, comparing notes in the school parking lot, and Laeticia had said, "Eleven fifty," the way she said prices, like it was nothing. Nevaeh had driven home with her hands at ten and two, doing the arithmetic at red lights. The same work. The same shelves, the same registers, practically the same parking lot asphalt.

Her first shift was a Tuesday. Mr. Tan gave her a green apron still warm from the dryer and showed her where the canned tomatoes lived, top shelf, back rows, and she stacked them until her shoulders burned in a way that felt less like pain and more like proof of something. At the end of the night he handed her a slip with her hours on it and said the checks came every two weeks, direct deposit if she filled out the form.

"You get eleven fifty?" she asked Laeticia at lunch the next day, sliding her tray down next to hers.

"For bagging. Same as you're doing." Laeticia pulled out her phone and showed a photo of her first pay stub, and Nevaeh read it twice, the way you reread a sentence that refuses to mean what it says. Eleven dollars and fifty cents per hour. She had done nothing differently. She had not interviewed better or negotiated or charmed anyone; she had simply been hired on one side of a line drawn somewhere in the woods between their towns.

She looked it up that night at the kitchen table while her mother watched something with sirens in it. The federal minimum wage was seven twenty-five an hour, and it had been seven twenty-five since July 24, 2009, which meant it was older than her little cousin. That was the floor, the legal bottom, the number her state had apparently decided was good enough. But states could set their own minimums, higher ones, and Laeticia's state had. Somewhere between the two capitals, someone had made a choice, and the choice was worth $4.25 an hour, which over a summer was a car payment, was the difference between saving for college and not saving at all.

She brought it up with Conner on Thursday, outside the gym, because Conner argued about everything and she wanted someone to argue with.

"So apply at Laeticia's store," he said, bouncing the basketball once, twice. "It's twenty minutes."

"It's not the store. It's the state. The federal one is seven twenty-five and it's been that since 2009, but states can go higher, and hers did. I checked."

Conner held the ball against his hip. "Then everyone here should just drive over there."

"And then what happens to this store? Who stocks the tomatoes?" She heard herself say it and then kept going, because the thought had only just arrived. "Mr. Tan's on some kind of sabbatical from his real job, he told me, teaching or something, he's just running the store for a year. If everyone quits for twenty minutes more an hour, the store doesn't close. It just hires people who can't drive over there."

The argument went around twice more and settled nowhere, which Conner seemed to find satisfying in itself. Nevaeh found it less satisfying. Her instinct, the first one, the visceral one, had been simple: it was unfair, and unfairness deserved a response, and the response was to quit and drive twenty minutes east. That was a clean position. She liked clean positions. But the second thought kept destabilizing the first, not because it was smarter but because it was truer to what she'd actually seen: the woman who trained her on the register, who had worked there nine years and arranged her shifts around a bus schedule that ran only every forty minutes; the high school kid who biked; Mr. Tan saying the green aprons were warm because the dryer was the one machine in the building that never broke. Driving to a higher number was easy for her. It was not equally easy for everyone standing next to her at the tomatoes.

She didn't quit that week. She filled out the direct deposit form, taped her schedule inside her locker at home, and on Sunday she worked a six-hour shift that ended with her sweeping the aisle where the tomatoes were, the overhead lights dimming in their long nightly sequence. Mr. Tan came by with the keys jangling in his fist and watched her work the broom into the corner.

"You'll get your first check Friday," he said. "Don't spend it all at once."

"Mr. Tan. Did you know seven twenty-five hasn't changed since 2009?"

He looked at her for a second, then at the aisle, then said, "The freezer truck comes at six in the morning. Don't block the loading dock when you park."

She propped the broom against the shelf, and outside, the parking lot was orange under the streetlight, her mother's car already idling by the cart corral.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
Brandon's grandmother had left the porch light on for him, though he had told her twice that he would not arrive before nine. The house smelled of coffee kept warm too long, and the table in the back room had been cleared of her puzzle magazines to make room for his laptop, his binder, and the two photocopied articles he had promised Mr. Van Dijk by Monday morning.

Both articles asked the same question: whether students who wrote practice essays throughout a term scored better on the final exam than students who did not. The first, by a team at a large university, had tested thousands of students and announced that the difference was statistically significant. The second, a smaller study of two hundred students at a liberal arts college, had found no significant difference and argued that the first study's enthusiasm was misplaced. Mr. Van Dijk had set the assignment with a certain dry pleasure, telling the class that a critical review meant holding the two papers against each other and deciding which one deserved their trust, or whether neither did.

Griffin had come along for the drive, ostensibly to see the lake before the weather turned, and now sat across the table peeling an orange while Brandon read the same paragraph for the third time. "Just say the big one wins," Griffin said, dropping rind into the empty candy dish. "More people, better math. That's what I'd write."

Brandon did not answer. In the margin of the first article, beside the word significant, he had written a question mark three days ago, and the mark had been bothering him since. He flipped to the results table and found the two averages: the essay writers had scored higher, yes, but when he converted the numbers the way the table allowed, the gap came out to something like a point and a half on a hundred-point exam.
