knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy.
story:
Benjamin's mother handed him the small silver cup on the way out the door, the way she might hand him car keys, and said his grandfather wanted him to do the Kiddush this year. All of it, she said, start to finish. He held the cup on his lap for the whole drive while his father found a parking spot three blocks from his aunt's house, because the street filled up early on nights like this.

He had practised in the car that afternoon, after school, in the back row of the student lot where nobody walked past. He knew the words from years of listening, the way he knew the words of songs he had never sung out loud, and when he finally said them alone with the windows up, his voice came out strange to him, too formal, like a person doing an impression of his grandfather. He tried again. The second time was better. The third time he stopped caring how it sounded and just said it, and the blessing settled into something he could carry.

At his aunt's house the table was already crowded when he arrived, cousins and second-cousins and the uncle from Lyon who always arrived belligerent about the parking and then softened by the second glass. The candles had been lit. His grandmother had polished the candlesticks until they held the light, and the silver cup in Benjamin's hand, when he set it down, looked dull by comparison, as though the years of his grandfather's thumbprints had burnished the old ones into something this one had not yet earned.

In the kitchen his cousin, who was nine, asked him what he was doing holding the cup like that, and he said, "The Kiddush. It's the blessing over the wine, or grape juice if you want, that starts the meal on Sabbath and festival nights. It marks the day as holy." She nodded and stole an olive. It was the first time he had said the whole fact out loud to another person, and saying it made him realize he had never quite understood it as a sentence before, only as a sound his grandfather made on Friday nights while everyone stood around the table with their heads bowed slightly, some of them just waiting for the food.

Before dinner his mother gave him an envelope. It had been in the cup, she said, tucked inside when she took it from the cabinet. The paper was thin and folded twice, and his grandfather's writing crossed it in the uneven lines of someone who wrote rarely and carefully. He asked Benjamin not to rush it. He said the blessing was not a performance, that he himself had gotten it wrong for years, treating it like a thing to get through. He said a theocracy could order a person to say words, and maybe even mean them, but nobody could order the words to mean something back. Benjamin read it twice and put it in his pocket.

That was the part he could not work out while his cousins argued about the seating and his aunt carried in the soup. His grandfather's note suggested two things at once: that the words only mattered if something in you answered them, and that he should not worry about whether anything answered. Benjamin stood by the window with the cup and thought about how he had practised. The first attempts had been performance, doing an impression. The last one had been something else, though he could not have said what. Maybe the answer his grandfather meant was not a feeling you checked for. Maybe it was just the difference between hurrying and not hurrying. He did not know, and he was tired of pretending to himself that he did.

Ulysse, who had come along because his own family was away, leaned against the counter beside him and asked if he was nervous. Benjamin said no, then said actually yes, a little. Ulysse said that when he had to recite a poem in front of class he imagined the audience as soup. Benjamin looked at the table, which was in fact mostly soup at this stage, and laughed harder than the joke deserved, and Etienne, who was arranging bread on a board, told them both to be quiet in a whisper that was louder than their laughing.

When the room quieted and his grandfather, seated at the far end, gave him the smallest nod, Benjamin lifted the cup. The wine caught the candlelight and moved a little because his hand was not perfectly still, and he let it move. He filled the blessing the way his grandfather filled pauses, without rushing, and when he reached the end the whole table said the response together, even the nine-year-old, even Ulysse, who had learned it by ear sometime during the soup.

His grandfather did not say it was good. He reached across the table, took the cup after Benjamin had drunk, poured a little more, and held it up toward the window where the night had gone fully dark. "Next year," he said, "you pour."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
story:
The reading room at the Roosevelt presidential library smelled of paper and lemon polish, and Charlotte had claimed the corner table by the window before the tour group arrived. She spread her notes across three folders: one for the revisionist argument that the United States had provoked the Cold War, one for the traditional view that the Soviets had started it, and one, still nearly empty, labeled in pencil with a question mark. On Saturday she would have to defend a position in Mr. Aziz's seminar debate, and by Wednesday she still did not know which position she could honestly defend.

Abigaelle dropped into the chair opposite her and slid a paper cup of vending machine coffee across the table. "You look like someone who lost a bet with a librarian."

"I lost a bet with myself," Charlotte said. She tapped the empty folder. "Every source I find picks a villain. Either Truman bullied the Soviets or Stalin betrayed everyone. My grandmother always said there's never just one person who ruins a family dinner."

"That's not a historiographical school, though."

"No," Charlotte admitted. "It's just my grandmother."

Down the corridor, the exhibit on the wartime alliance gleamed under low lights: a photograph of Tehran, a decoded cable, Roosevelt's wheelchair tucked behind a velvet rope. Addyson came through the doorway with her phone in one hand and a bound volume in the other, breathless and nonchalant at once, the way she got when she'd found something. "Microfilm room. Nobody goes in there. Look." She set the volume on the table. It was a library copy of John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book, The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947, its spine cracked, a due date card stamped with names from decades past.

Charlotte turned to the sections she'd flagged from the index and read in silence for a while. The argument assembled itself slowly, paragraph by paragraph: Gaddis refused to lay the whole thing at either door. Neither side, he maintained, could bear sole responsibility. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it was so plain it seemed almost like a trick. She had spent two weeks trying to codify her notes into a verdict, and here was a scholar who had built a whole book on declining to give one.

"So what do you call someone who blames both sides?" Addyson asked, peering over her arm.

"Post-revisionist," Charlotte said. "That's the word for the view. Post-revisionism."

"You made that up."

"I didn't. It's in the review essays, back here, look." She turned the pages toward the window light. "The revisionists came first, saying the U.S. caused it. Then people pushed back against that, and Gaddis ended up in this middle country nobody wanted to live in."

Mr. Aziz appeared at the table a little later, visitor badge clipped to his jacket, having come for the archive tour himself. He listened while Charlotte laid out her problem: the evidence of Soviet behavior in Eastern Europe, the evidence of American unilateralism at Hiroshima and in the atom diplomacy, the temptation each side had felt to see the other as an irreducible enemy. She spoke faster as she went, laying the two explanations side by side and then, for the first time, refusing to slide either one off the table. He asked her two questions, offered no verdicts, and told her the reading room closed at four.

She stayed until ten minutes before four. What she wrote in the once-empty folder was not a conclusion but a way of standing: the security dilemma was real, the ideological rivalry was real, and the record did not permit her to weigh them to the last gram. Some things about the Cold War she would claim with confidence on Saturday; others she would have to say she did not know, out loud, in front of people who might read uncertainty as weakness. She found she minded that less than she had on Monday.

When the archivist began switching off the gallery lights, the photograph of Tehran went dim, the three men at their table dissolving into shadow. Charlotte squared her folders, slid the Gaddis volume into her bag to re-shelve at the desk, and followed the others toward the entrance. Outside, the autumn lawn stretched down toward the river, and Abigaelle asked what she would open with on Saturday.

Charlotte pulled her jacket closed against the wind. "Neither side could bear sole responsibility," she said. "I'll just start there and see what happens."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Borrowing $300,000 for 30 years at a fixed 6 percent rate means paying more than $347,000 in interest, more than the amount borrowed.
story:
The apartment was on the third floor of a brick walk-up, and Amy counted the stairs on the way up because the listing said "charming" and she had learned that charming meant stairs. The agent unlocked the door and stood back. Two bedrooms, a kitchen with a window over the sink, a radiator that clanked when the agent bumped it with her hip. Amy walked to the window. From here she could see the laundromat and the corner where the bus turned, which meant she could get to campus in twenty minutes without transferring.

Isabelle came in behind her, carrying her coat over one arm even though it was cold in the hallway. "I call the back bedroom," she said.

"You haven't even seen it."

"I don't need to see it. It's farther from the radiator. You're always hot. This is symbiosis, Amy. You get the heat, I get the quiet." Isabelle opened the back bedroom's door, frowned at a water stain on the ceiling, and said nothing about it, which Amy noted.

The agent, a woman with a lanyard and a phone that kept buzzing, laid a folder on the kitchen counter. "So the numbers. Rent's fourteen hundred a month. To move in you need first month, last month, and a security deposit, so forty-two hundred total. Some landlords call it first, last, and security." She said it fast, the way she'd said it to a hundred people.

Amy had thirty-one hundred in her account. She had been saving since September, birthday money and the flower shop shifts, and she had watched the total climb in a way that had felt like progress until this moment. "Is there any flexibility on the deposit?"

"None from this owner, sorry." The agent flipped a page. "Actually, and I have to disclose this, the owner is also considering selling the unit. If someone buys, your lease would transfer, but there's a chance a buyer wants to occupy."

"When you say selling," Amy said, "how much would a place like this go for?"

The agent glanced at the folder. "This building, that unit, around three hundred thousand."

Amy took out her phone. She opened a mortgage calculator because she had heard the word her whole life without ever holding one, and she typed in the numbers: three hundred thousand, thirty years, fixed rate, six percent. Below the loan amount the screen showed the total interest, and she looked at it, and looked at it again. More than three hundred forty-seven thousand dollars. More than the borrowed amount itself. She would hand over six hundred and forty-seven thousand dollars, over three decades, to borrow three hundred thousand, and at the end of it the radiator and the water stain and the stairs would be hers.

"Twenty-eight years from now," Amy said, still looking at the screen, "I'd be forty-six. And the interest alone would be bigger than the loan."

"What?" Isabelle came over and leaned on her shoulder to read. "That can't be right. You're saying the bank makes more than the house costs."

"That's what it says. Borrowing three hundred thousand for thirty years at six percent fixed, and the interest is more than three hundred and forty-seven thousand." She turned the phone so Isabelle could see the total line, the plain arithmetic of it, no room for interpretation.

Isabelle went quiet for a second, which was unusual. "My parents have a mortgage," she said. "Thirty years, they complain about it at dinner like it's weather. I never thought about what it adds up to." She walked back toward the bedrooms, then stopped in the doorway. "But rent is fourteen hundred a month and it's gone. At least the mortgage people end up with a building."

"They end up with it when they're almost fifty," Amy said. "If nothing goes wrong. If the roof doesn't go and the job doesn't go." She thought of her mother recuperating on the couch for all of October after the surgery, the shifts she hadn't been able to pick up, how fast a savings account could flatten. Thirty years was a long time to promise anything, and the interest number was a promise, written down before anything went wrong.

The agent's phone buzzed again and she stepped into the hallway to answer it. Amy stood at the kitchen window. Down on the sidewalk a man was taping a FOR SALE sign to the fence beside the laundromat, smoothing the tape with his thumb, twice, three times, until it lay flat.

"Here's the thing," Isabelle said from the doorway, quieter now. "I want this apartment. I want the back bedroom and the twenty-minute bus and to not live in the dorms with two hundred other people who steal my yogurt. I have eleven hundred. Together that's forty-two hundred exactly, to the dollar, and then we have nothing until my next paycheck, which is nine days."

"You'd be in for the whole lease? Not just kind of in?"

"In. Fully. If the deposit counts me the same as you, I'm on the paperwork today." Isabelle had never committed to anything for longer than a season, and they both knew it, and the offer sat in the air being weighed.

The agent came back in. "So, you want to apply? I'll need the deposit at signing, and there's a credit check, twenty-five dollars each."

Amy looked at the water stain on the ceiling of the back bedroom, at the radiator, at Isabelle, who had crossed the kitchen and was standing by the window with her hand flat on the counter like she was claiming it. Six hundred and forty-seven thousand dollars over thirty years, or fourteen hundred a month into nothing, and a deposit that would empty both of them to the dollar. She could not see which one was the sensible choice. She could only see that one of them had to be made before the agent's phone buzzed again.

"We'll apply," Amy said, and pulled out her debit card for the credit check.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
Ella arrived at Marlowe Park an hour before the guests, carrying two crates of small clay lamps that her mother had wrapped in newspaper like eggs. The pavilion by the duck pond had been reserved since September, and already her aunts were unrolling paper tablecloths and arguing about whether the samosas should go beside the sweets or across from them, a dispute with the gravity of a border negotiation.

Her phone buzzed on the folding table. A message from Ilias, who had moved here in June and had never heard of any of this: "so what actually IS Diwali? douglas says fireworks, my mom says lamps, the internet says like five different religions??"

Ella crouched beside the crates while she typed. She knew the answer the way she knew her own address, without having to think, but typing it made her look at it. She wrote back: "lamps. we light these little oil lamps called diyas, in homes and temples. that's the whole point, light winning over darkness. and it's not just us, hindus, jains, sikhs, and some buddhists all celebrate it. douglas isn't wrong about fireworks either, he's just wrong about everything else."

"wait," Ilias replied, "YOU have a religion?"

That was the question, she supposed, dressed in its usual rude clothing. She set the phone face down and began filling the diyas from a plastic bottle of oil, wicks first, then a thin pool for each, her fingers going glossy. Around her the pavilion smelled of cardamom and frying dough and the cold green smell of the pond. A duck sidestepped along the bank with the offended air of a party guest who had not been invited.

What she wanted, if she was honest, was to be somewhere unclaimed for one night. In eleven days she would be on a campus three states away where nobody knew her aunts or her mother's reputation for coconut burfi, and the thought of that blankness felt like a reprieve, like a door left open onto a quiet hallway. She had told Douglas she might meet him and the others at the bowling alley after the lamps were lit. She had even chosen the outfit. Freedom, her history teacher liked to say, does not emancipate anyone by itself; you have to walk out on your own legs. Ella had written that down in March and underlined it twice, which now seemed embarrassing.

"Rows," her grandmother said, pressing a diya into her hands. "Along the edges, all the way to the path, so the light finds people coming." Her grandmother did not explain things. She pointed at the pavilion posts, at the railing, at the crooked line of the gravel path, and Ella carried the lamps two at a time and placed them, adjusting each one on the uneven ground so it sat level, thinking that the oil would spill if the clay tilted, thinking that she was taking this more seriously than she took most of her homework.

Then the wind came off the pond, sudden and sideways, and the matchbox in her pocket turned out to be damp, impermeable to every strike. Her aunt produced a lighter from somewhere in her cardigan, and her mother sent her cousin sprinting to the car for backup matches, and for a few minutes the pavilion was pure comedy: four adults and Ella crouched in a defensive huddle around one guttering flame, shielding it with their bodies like soldiers around a fallen flag, while the duck watched from the water with what could only be described as satisfaction. "The darkness is winning," her aunt announced, deadpan, and her grandmother said, "Not for long," and nobody needed to say anything else about it.

They got the diyas lit just as the first guests came up the path, and the sight of it stopped Ella halfway through striking another match. The little flames ran in a broken gold line down the railing and along the ground, doubled and wobbling in the pond, and the dark had not vanished, of course. The dark was still everywhere behind the lamps, between them, out past the trees where the bowling alley was. But the light was winning where it stood. She took out her phone to text Douglas that she wasn't coming, and found Ilias's last message still unanswered, the cursor blinking after "YOU have a religion?"

She typed, "no. I have lamps," sent it, and put the phone in her pocket with the dead matches. Then she picked up two more diyas and carried them toward the far end of the path, where the line of light had not yet reached.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
The coffee shop on Delancey Street had become, over one long October weekend, Hailey's second home, mostly because it was warm and because Miguel worked the espresso machine on Sundays and slipped her extra whipped cream without being asked. She had turned eighteen in September, which meant that on Tuesday she would vote for the first time, and she had the sample ballot folded into her jacket pocket like a secret she kept touching to make sure it was real.

"I still don't get why you're agonizing," Miguel said, sliding a cappuccino across the counter. "It's one vote. My cousin says young people barely show up anyway. Half of them, tops, something like that, and that's in a big year."

"That's exactly why it matters," Evangeline said from the window seat, where she was highlighting a pamphlet with the intensity of someone defusing a bomb. "If half of us stay home, the half that shows up speaks for everybody." Miguel rolled his eyes and began steaming milk with unnecessary violence.

Hailey sipped her drink and didn't answer, because the truth was she could argue both sides, and did, silently, all the way home. Miguel wasn't wrong that a single vote vanished into the millions like a drop of rain into a lake. But Evangeline's version had its own gravity: the drop was still water, still counted when the lake was measured. She wanted to hold both ideas at once, and they refused to sit still together, like cats in the same crate.

On Monday she went back to the coffee shop to study and found Ms. Islam, her old neighbor from fourth grade, at the corner table with a laptop and a stack of flyers about the city's new parking ordinance, which Hailey had skimmed in the local paper and found interminable. "Come sit," Ms. Islam said. "You look like a girl with a question." Hailey did have one, though it took her two sips of cocoa to find it. "Do you know how many young people actually vote? Miguel said half, but he heard it from his cousin."

Ms. Islam turned her laptop around without a word. On the screen was a page from CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, and Hailey read the line twice: they estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election. Fifty percent, a big presidential year, the best kind of year, and still only half. "Huh," she said. "Miguel was right by accident." Ms. Islam smiled into her tea and offered no commentary, which Hailey appreciated, because she wanted to work this out herself and hated when adults expatiated on a topic she hadn't finished chewing.

What I realized, sitting there with the cocoa going cold, was that Miguel and Evangeline had been arguing about the same number in two different moods. He saw the fifty percent who stayed home and thought, why bother joining the ones who show up, the drop is so small. She saw the fifty percent who showed up and thought, imagine if the other half came too. The number hadn't changed. Only the direction you walked around it. It was like the parking ordinance pamphlets stacked on Ms. Islam's table: dry, tedious, and yet somebody's whole afternoon depended on whether the permit fee went up. Small boring things added up to the shape of a town, or a country, or at least I couldn't prove they didn't.

Tuesday morning I walked to the polling place at the elementary school with Evangeline, who had made us both wear her homemade stickers that said I VOTED BEFORE MY LATTE, which the polling volunteers found either charming or gratuitous, hard to tell. The line was short at seven. A woman with a lanyard checked my name against a binder, and there was a small ceremonial thrill in hearing her say it back to me, Hailey, registered, confirmed, like the state had finally learned my name.

In the booth I stood with the ballot and my pencil hovering, and I thought of Miguel and his whipped cream, and of the fifty percent, and of how I still wasn't sure one pencil mark could matter in a country so wide. But I was sure of this: I was one of the ones who showed up, and that was a fact now, not an argument. I filled in the first bubble, then the next, and my hand was steadier than I expected. Behind me, through the gym doors, Evangeline called out, "Hurry up, the coffee shop opens in ten minutes and Miguel promised us free whipped cream for civic participation."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The parking lot of the Crestwood Funeral Home was still half full when Katherine slid into the back seat of her mother's car and pulled the door shut. Her tights itched. On the seat beside her lay her grandmother's cardigan, folded the way her mother folded things at moments like this, as if neatness could underpin the shape of the afternoon. Her mother started the engine but didn't put the car in gear.

"Everyone's going back to Aunt Carol's," her mother said. "There's food. People expect us."

"I can't sit in a room for three more hours while people tell me she looks peaceful."

"She does look peaceful."

"That's the point. She's dead and she looks peaceful. It's the worst sentence in the English language." Katherine heard her own voice go sharp, almost belligerent, and she didn't like it, but she couldn't soften it either.

Her mother put the car in drive. They pulled out onto the county road, past the church where Katherine had been baptized and where her grandmother had, until February, played organ every Sunday. Neither of them spoke. The fields were pale with late corn stubble. Katherine took out her phone, not to look at anything in particular, and found a text from Marisa, sent during the service: I know you're at the funeral. You don't have to answer. But Taylor's party is tonight and I saved you a spot on the couch even though you always steal the blankets.

She stared at it. She had laughed at something yesterday, an old episode of a show her grandmother had hated, and the laugh had come out of her so easily that she'd felt like a traitor. Her grandmother had been dead four days. How could a body laugh four days out? At the reception after the burial she'd eaten two rolls and enjoyed them, and then she'd stood in the corner afterward and hated herself with a completeness that felt almost religious.

She typed back: Can I ask you something weird.

Marisa answered fast, because Marisa always answered fast: I'm in physics. Ask.

Is it messed up to go to a party a week after a funeral. Like if I actually have fun.

There was a pause long enough for Katherine to watch a grain truck pass them going the other way. Then: ok so my psych textbook from last semester is in my locker for some reason, hold on.

Her mother glanced in the mirror. "Who's that?"

"Marisa. She's helping me with something." Katherine didn't specify. Her mother's hands were tight on the wheel and Katherine understood, in some wordless way, that her mother was also deciding whether to face the day or merely survive it.

The phone buzzed with a photo: a page with a diagram, two circles like a broken figure eight, arrows looping between them. Under it Marisa had typed: it's called the dual process model. it's by Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut. it says grieving people move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life. not one direction. it's not a straight line out the other side. So no, it's not messed up. It's literally the model.

Katherine read it twice. The arrows went both ways. Restoration on one side, confrontation on the other, and a person supposed to travel between them, again and again, without apology. It was not an encapsulation of her week exactly, nothing could be, but it was close enough that she exhaled for what felt like the first time since Tuesday.

"So Taylor's at nine," she said out loud.

Her mother's shoulders dropped maybe half an inch. "You want to go to a party tonight?"

"I don't know. Maybe for an hour. And then maybe I'll come home and be sad in the kitchen with you." She watched the mirror. "Apparently that's allowed. Moving back and forth. Marisa sent me this thing from her psych book."

"Back and forth," her mother repeated, as if testing the phrase against her own ribs.

"Stroebe and Schut. It's a real model, not a Tumblr thing." Katherine set the phone face down on her knee. "I still feel like I'm doing it wrong, whatever it is. That part doesn't go away."

At the turn for Aunt Carol's subdivision, her mother kept the car straight. "One loop past the lake," she said. "Then we'll go in. I can't sit in that room either, and somebody has to admit it first." The lake came up on the left, gray and evenly wind-brushed, a single canoe pulled up on the grass. They rode past it slowly, her mother easing off the gas without stopping.

Katherine rolled the window down an inch, just enough for cold air to thread through the car and stir the cardigan on the seat. She texted Marisa: save the blankets. coming at nine.

"An hour," her mother said.

"One and a half," said Katherine, and her mother laughed, short and cracked and real, and turned the car around at the next road to go and face the aunts.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
Kate had told everyone she was fine, and by the third week she had almost convinced herself, except that she was standing in the Fairlane Cemetery at nine in the morning with a tin of lemon squares she had no plan for. The grass was still wet. Her grandmother had been in the ground since the seventeenth, which was a thing Kate refused to phrase that way out loud, and yet she kept phrasing it that way in her head, testing the sentence like a loose tooth.

Her mother had dropped her at the gate and said she'd circle back in an hour. Daxton had offered to come, twice, and she had said no, twice, and then he showed up anyway at the edge of the plot with his hands in his pockets and a bakery bag from the place on Route 9. He wanted to be useful. He had wanted to be useful since the funeral, carrying chairs, refilling ice, and Kate understood that this was his way of holding on to a friendship he suspected she was quietly ending, though she would not have admitted she was doing any such thing.

"You brought cookies," she said.

"Scones. There's a difference. I'm something of a connoisseur at this point, my mom keeps buying them." He set the bag on the flat granite marker, next to her tin. "You didn't have to bring anything."

"She'd want them eaten, though. That's the problem."

They sat on the low stone wall that bordered the older section, where the graves went back to 1904 and the pines gave the whole acreage a boreal hush, cooler and darker than the parking lot below. Kate told him the thing she hadn't told her mother: that she still cooked from the recipe cards. That last Sunday she'd made the chicken with forty cloves and had said, out loud, at the stove, "You always said watch the garlic, don't let it go bitter," and then had stood there feeling like a person who should be evaluated.

"That's not weird," Daxton said.

"You impute normalcy to everything I do. It's your whole personality."

"Fine, it's a little weird. My therapist says my uncle still sets a plate at Thanksgiving. Six years. Nobody says anything about it." He pulled a scone apart and left half in the bag. "Anyway I looked it up. There's this book from 1996, Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman. It argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on."

Kate looked at him. "You looked it up."

"You said the thing about the garlic at the stove, like, three weeks ago, and you looked so embarrassed I figured I should check whether you were losing it." He shrugged. "You're not. Or everybody is, together."

She took out her phone and found it herself, the library copy, hold request placed before she had finished deciding to. That was the part she would not tell her mother either: that she had spent forty minutes that night reading the first chapter at the kitchen table, with the recipe box still open beside her, and had gone to bed feeling something she could only describe as permission, though permission from whom she couldn't say.

Here was what she hadn't told anyone. She had told her mother the lemon squares were for the neighbor, Mr. Georgiou, whose mower she'd been using all summer, and that was half true, she did owe him something. But she had also told her mother she was over the worst of it, and that morning in the bathroom mirror she had rehearsed a face that matched the claim, and she had walked past the recipe box to leave without touching it, and then had turned around at the door and taken the cards, all of them, rubber-banded, and put them in her bag, where they were right now, pressing against her spine.

At the wall, Daxton checked the time. "Your mom's going to be at the gate."

"In a minute." Kate opened the tin and set one lemon square on the marker, which she knew was a gesture for her and not for anyone else, and which she intended to keep making, Sundays, when she came, because she intended to keep coming. She didn't know yet how to hold both things, that the dead are gone and that they are not gone, but the book had a shelf mark and she had a library card and there was no deadline. She picked up the bakery bag and held it out to him. "Take the scones to Mr. Georgiou. Tell him thanks for the mower, and that I'll bring the real ones next week, the ones with the card."

Daxton took the bag. "What's the card say?"

"Watch the garlic," Kate said, and closed the tin.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The article came from a German news site Hafsa's mother kept open on the kitchen tablet, and it was only four paragraphs long, which was why Alexia had agreed to try it in the first place. She sat at the counter with a printed copy, a pencil, and the sliding feeling that she had promised more than she could deliver. In two weeks she had to stand up in Mr. Asante's class and summarise a German news article aloud, from memory, and so far she could count her German words on her fingers and still have fingers left over.

Hafsa set down two glasses of mint tea and leaned over her shoulder. "Okay, first sentence. Read it to me. Don't stop."

Alexia read. It was slow, and the sounds came out flat where they should have rounded. Halfway through she stopped, frowning at the page.

"Why are there so many capitals? It looks like the whole sentence is shouting." She pointed at the second line, where three words in a row began with big letters, none of them anyone's name as far as she could tell. "Is that a mistake in the printing?"

Hafsa laughed and pulled out the stool beside her. "Not a mistake. German capitalizes every noun, not only names. That's just how it is." She tapped the page. "Look again."

Alexia looked again, and something rearranged itself behind her eyes. The capitals were not noise; they were a map. Wherever a word rose up in a big letter, there was a noun, and if she could find the nouns, she could find what the sentence was actually about, like following stones across a river. She went through the first paragraph with her pencil, underlining every capitalized word that was not at the start of a sentence, and a small heap of meanings began to gather: Stadt, Frau, Bus. City, woman, bus. She did not know the verbs yet, but she knew who was in the story and where it was happening, and that was more than she had managed in an hour of staring at the page before Hafsa had invited her over.

"This actually helps," she said, surprised at how the discovery seemed to invigorate her, the way cold water does when you stop dreading it and drink it. "The article's about a bus driver. A woman bus driver, maybe, in some city."

"See if the second paragraph agrees with you," Hafsa said.

The doorbell rang, and it was Deegan, who had walked over with his own assignment half-finished and a bag of sour candies. He dropped into the chair across from them and read the title upside down. "You're doing the Asante thing? He told me summarising is the easy option. You just say what the article says."

"It's not easy," Alexia said, and heard how petulant it came out, so she softened it. "It's not easy in a language where I know forty words."

Deegan unwrapped a candy with great ceremony. "Then cheat a little. Memorise one sentence, say it, and then say the rest in English. He won't know."

"He'll know," Hafsa said.

"He might not."

Alexia turned back to the page, because the argument was sliding somewhere she did not want to go. The second paragraph had more capitals, more nouns lined up like streetlights, and she worked through them with the dictionary Hafsa's mother lent them, an old one with a cracked spine that smelled faintly of dust and cardamom. Phonetics she could not manage; she wrote the words out in her own private spelling, tsair for the one that meant time, and practised them in a mutter while Deegan, despite himself, started underlining nouns in the third paragraph too.

Then she hit a word that broke her system. It began with a capital, sat in the middle of the sentence, and was not in the dictionary under any spelling she tried. She turned the page toward the window light. "Hafsa, this one. What is it?"

Hafsa looked, and then laughed so hard she had to set her tea down. "That's the woman's name. It's a person, not a thing. The bus driver's name."

Alexia stared at it, and the twist of it settled over her slowly and then, unexpectedly, pleasantly. Her map had a flaw: it showed her all the nouns, but it could not tell her which nouns were people. She had spent twenty minutes trusting the capitals to mean one thing, and now she understood they meant the thing and also its shadow, the name attached to the thing. Frau Weber was a woman and also a Weber, and the article was suddenly not about a bus driver at all but about a specific person, someone who had driven the same route for years, and the third paragraph's nouns, when she looked at them newly, were years, route, passengers. People who rode her bus.

Deegan leaned over. "So what's it about?"

Alexia closed the dictionary. "A woman named Weber drives a bus. I think she's retiring. I think that's why it's news." She was honest enough with herself to admit she was not certain; the last paragraph still sat there unread, its capitals waiting.

"Say it in German," Hafsa said. "Just that much. Out loud."

Alexia took a breath and said it, slowly, the flat sounds rounding a little on the second try. Then she picked up her pencil and went back to the last paragraph, underlining capitals, one by one.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Julia had been told, in her first coaching meeting at the community pool, that the twelve-year-olds' passing was the problem. She stood at the shallow end with a clipboard she had bought that morning and watched them fumble a simple water polo drill, the ball slapping flat against the water instead of arriving in a teammate's raised hand. Mr. Szabó, the head coach who had recruited her from the senior team, had been precise about the weakness and vague about everything else. "You plan the drills," he said. "You fix it. I'll be at the far lanes with the swimmers."

Her first plan came out of everything she knew as a player, which meant correction, constant and immediate. When Abdullah's little brother dropped a pass, she told him why before the splash had settled. Elbow high. Follow through toward the target. Lead the receiver, don't throw at them. She was, she realized on the second evening, becoming loquacious in a way she never was in person, narrating every attempt, filling the gaps between drills with instruction. The kids nodded. They performed the fixes while she stood at the edge and said the words. Their passing got cleaner, and she felt the small pleasure of being the reason for something.

Then came the Saturday scrimmage against the team from the next town. Julia stood on the deck, mouth open, and watched her careful work dissolve. Passes died mid-water. The elbow dropped, the lead vanished, and by the third quarter the kids had stopped looking at each other at all. Vaughn, who played keeper and had come to watch his cousin, leaned on the rail beside her. "They only pass when you talk," he said, not unkindly. "You could hear the silence from up here."

She wanted to argue, and the argument rose in her with real force, because she had worked, because the drills had worked, because she had the clipboard to prove it. But the score was what it was. On the bus back, Abdullah's brother sat with his hood up and wouldn't say what was wrong, and when Abdullah pressed him he said only, "Out there she can't tell me." Julia looked out the window at the parking lots going by and understood that she had built something that required her voice as one of its parts.

That night she searched, half-ashamed, through coaching forums and old syllabi she found linked from a college course page, chasing the memory of something a former coach of hers had once muttered at a whiteboard. There was a name for it. She wrote the phrase in the margin of her drill sheet and then, feeling slightly fraudulent, as though owning the words might be a kind of circumlocution for the fact that she simply didn't know what to do, she wrote underneath it a question: less of me, but how much less?

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," she told Mr. Szabó on Monday, before she could soften it into something safer. He looked at her over his coffee. "Feedback after every attempt can make them dependent on it," she said. "Less frequent feedback helps retention." He considered this, and she braced for correction, for the adult version of the truth to replace hers. Instead he said, "So what's the plan?" and it was somehow worse, because now the plan had to be hers.

She rebuilt the week in halves. On Tuesday she coached as before, correction after correction, elbow high, lead the receiver. On Thursday she sat on a folding chair behind the goal and said nothing at all. The first ten minutes were chaos, kids glancing at her, passes wobbling, one boy near tears of frustration. Then, slowly, they began coaching themselves. Abdullah's brother stopped a bad pass by catching it against his chest, looked at his own hands, and threw the next one flatter and harder. Julia kept her mouth shut until it ached, and by the end of the session they had found something, imperfectly, that they could not have found while she was speaking.

She did not believe the solution was that clean. Some of the kids, she suspected, were drowning in the silence rather than learning from it; one girl named nothing in Julia's notes, only "red cap, cries easily," had looked more lost on Thursday than ever. Maybe the right amount of feedback was different for each of them, or changed week to week, or depended on things she couldn't see. She wrote both columns in her notebook, the talking days and the silent days, and left a third column blank because she didn't yet know what it was for.
